planting.note: Plant bulbs 2-3 inches deep and 4-6 inches apart in lean, fast-draining soil in fall so roots establish before winter. Choose a hot, exposed spot such as a rock garden or gravel bed, since this onion comes from thin, rocky Piedmont and sandhills soils and resents heavy, wet clay.

directions: This small southeastern bulb produces grass-like foliage in late winter and sends up a slender scape topped with a tight ball of white-to-lavender starry flowers in late spring. Striped papery bulb coats and a crested seed capsule distinguish it from other eastern wild onions. Let the foliage yellow and die back naturally after bloom, since the bulb needs a dry summer dormancy similar to its native thin rock-outcrop and sandhill soils. Division of offset bulbs in late summer dormancy is the most reliable way to increase a clump once established.
sources: Flora of the Southeastern United States (FSUS)
